card.hook: Picture a calm Venice morning: one big stone arch, tiny shops tucked into its span, and the whole thing doubled in the Grand Canal while a vaporetto slides past. That's the Rialto, and it's much easier to photograph than you'd expect.
card.stand_here: Head for Riva del Vin on the San Polo (south-west) bank, the canal-side street. Face the bridge side-on; it's to the east of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole arch side-on. Go to 0.5x if you want more canal and boats, or try zoom 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for a tighter shot of the arch and its shops.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the waterline on the lower third and keep the phone level, because the long line of the bridge shows every tilt.
card.best_time: Aim for sunrise (about 6:30-7:30) or the blue hour, when the water is usually calm and the reflections are clearest. Riva del Vin can be crowded by midday. In the blue hour, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on something steady, because boats move and will blur.
card.selfie_here: Find the small corner of land jutting out toward the Grand Canal, right next to the Al Buso restaurant. Use the front camera, switch to the wider setting if your phone has one, and let the bridge rise up behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the dock at the foot of the bridge on the San Polo side (after you come down off the bridge, turn right and follow the buildings), then pose with the bridge in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Step aside so you don't block people crossing the bridge, respect the vendors and their workspace, skip the flash, and don't sit on the bridge steps to eat. Keep out of the way of any boats parking at the wooden docks.
card.challenge: Wait for a boat to drift into a gap and catch it under the arch, with a strip of water in front, and no boat cutting across the bridge.
card.good_to_know: The Rialto is the oldest of the four bridges across the Grand Canal. Antonio da Ponte built the single broad stone arch between 1588 and 1591, and it was thought so daring that one architect predicted it would fall down. It has now stood for more than four centuries, after earlier crossings that included a floating pontoon bridge and a wooden one that collapsed more than once.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Riva del Vin on the San Polo (south-west) bank, the canal-side street. Face the bridge side-on; it's to the east of you.

card.hook: Everyone queues up for the Bridge of Sighs expecting a grand, sweeping thing, then discovers it's small, pale and tucked between two big buildings. That's exactly why it makes such a neat photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ponte della Paglia, right by the Doge's Palace, and look north up the Rio di Palazzo. The bridge will be right in front of you, with the palace on one side and the New Prison on the other.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the bridge sits nicely between the two buildings. Then try zoom 2x (a bit more on some phones) to pick out the stone windows and the row of carved heads. Zoom 0.5x fits in more palace, but the bridge ends up looking tiny and the crowd looks huge.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white stone of the bridge, and if the sky or water is washing it out, slide the brightness down a touch.
card.best_time: Go early, around sunrise (about 6:00-8:00am), when the crowds are thinnest. Late afternoon is also a good shout. Midday is the hardest time to get a clear frame, because the crowds build from mid-morning.
card.selfie_here: Head down from Ponte della Paglia to the small platform that wraps around the corner of the building, below and to the right of the bridge. Use the front camera with the Bridge of Sighs over your shoulder. Another option is the small concrete dock just past Ponte della Paglia (cross the bridge, then turn left), where you're right at the water's edge. These two might turn out to be the same spot, so have a look when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the small Ponte Larga S. Marco while you stand on Ponte de la Canonica, so the Bridge of Sighs appears behind you (check the arch fits in the frame before they take it).
card.rules_and_safety: Ponte della Paglia is a public bridge, free and open at all hours, but you may have to climb a few small steps. Going inside the Bridge of Sighs is part of the Doge's Palace visit, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Wait for a gondola to glide under the arch, then catch it with a quick burst and see if you can get the gondolier and the bridge both looking their best.
card.good_to_know: The Bridge of Sighs is made of white Istrian limestone and links the Doge's Palace with the New Prison. It was designed by Antonio Contin and built soon after 1600. Inside are two separate walkways, which kept prisoners heading to court apart from those already convicted. The romantic name is a 19th-century invention, given in English by Lord Byron.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ponte della Paglia, right by the Doge's Palace, and look north up the Rio di Palazzo. The bridge will be right in front of you, with the palace on one side and the New Prison on the other.

selfie_spots.why: A ledge off the covered walkway below the bridge gives a visitor a photo with the Bridge of Sighs behind them.

The Oxford Bridge of Sighs results were ignored because they are a different landmark.

card.hook: Picture a little bridge packed with people all holding their phones up at the same stone bridge. That's Ponte della Paglia, and the view is worth the wait: a Gothic palace corner, a canal, and the enclosed Bridge of Sighs.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ponte della Paglia, the bridge beside the Doge's Palace's south-east corner, over the Rio di Palazzo. Face the palace's waterside corner so the Bridge of Sighs is across the canal in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the palace corner and the Bridge of Sighs together. If the bridge is crowded and you can't step back, try 0.5x. For a tighter shot of the Bridge of Sighs, go to 2x or higher, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the palace corner up with one of the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, though the bridge is never empty. Take a few shots in a row and keep the one where people have drifted out of the way.
card.selfie_here: Head into Piazza San Marco and find the lamp post by the palace exit. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and pose with the palace and St Mark's Basilica filling the background behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: For the whole palace, ask a passer-by to stand near the middle of Piazza San Marco facing the palace, so the full length of the facade fits in the frame, while you pose in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The outside views are free from the street, but the inside views, like the Giants' Staircase, need a palace ticket. Check the official site before you go, including its current photo rules.
card.challenge: Put the palace corner on a gridline, keep the Bridge of Sighs in the top of the frame with a strip of water below, and wait for a gap in the crowd. Bonus points if you get it without a single stranger.
card.good_to_know: The Doge's Palace was once the Doge's home, and it also held government offices and a jail. A first palace was built in 810, the Gothic rebuilding began around 1340, and it has been a museum since 1923. The enclosed Bridge of Sighs has linked the palace to the prison since the 16th century.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ponte della Paglia, the bridge beside the Doge's Palace's south-east corner, over the Rio di Palazzo. Face the palace's waterside corner so the Bridge of Sighs is across the canal in front of you.

card.hook: Most squares make you pick one thing to photograph. Piazza San Marco puts the basilica, the arcades and a free-standing bell tower in a single frame, so the only hard part is choosing where to stand.
card.stand_here: Take the lift up the Campanile di San Marco and stand at the top, then face out over the square toward the Doge's Palace, the basilica roofs and the lagoon. If you'd rather stay at water level, Punta della Dogana across the water shows the square, the Doge's Palace and the Campanile together.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole square and the lagoon in. Then try 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out the Doge's Palace, the basilica roofs or boats on the water. Zoom 1x is the easy, balanced choice.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, then tap the square and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: For the ground-level view, some guides say go early, before about 8 AM, because stalls and crowds build up after that. For the tower view, check the official site for current times before you go.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x, hold your phone a bit higher than usual and tilt it up slightly. That way you get a big landmark over your shoulder instead of just a forehead.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open public space, but the Campanile lift is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Zoom to 5x from the top and find a boat on the lagoon, then catch it in a photo before it slips out of frame.
card.good_to_know: The Campanile dates from 1156-73. It collapsed on 14 July 1902 and was rebuilt in 1912 'as it was, where it was'. The Clocktower, finished in 1499, marks the start of the Merceria shopping route towards the Rialto.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Take the lift up the Campanile di San Marco and stand at the top, then face out over the square toward the Doge's Palace, the basilica roofs and the lagoon. If you'd rather stay at water level, Punta della Dogana across the water shows the square, the Doge's Palace and the Campanile together.

card.hook: Five arched doorways, a wall of gold mosaics and four bronze horses are all trying to get into your photo at once. Luckily, they fit.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open paving in the middle of Piazza San Marco, between the Campanile and the basilica. The basilica is about 95 m to the east, so face east and you'll see the whole front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the basilica, the Campanile and the arcades into one shot. Switch to 1x for a cleaner view of the front alone, then zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the mosaics, the portals and the horses.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and keep the basilica centred so the vertical lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Go early, before about 8:00 to 9:00. The square is emptier and the light is softer, so you get the gold without the crowds.
card.selfie_here: Find the street lamp in front of the Doge's Palace exit and pose by the pole with the basilica and palace behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x so more of the building squeezes in over your shoulder, and have fun with the pose.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of the square, about 80-100 m from the front and centred on the main portal, while you pose in their view so all five arches fit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography isn't allowed inside the basilica, and that includes phones and selfies in front of interior features, so make the square your main picture. The Loggia dei Cavalli may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole front, then zoom in and find all four bronze horses above the entrance. Bonus points if you spot them before your friends do.
card.good_to_know: St Mark's is the cathedral church of Venice and holds the relics of Saint Mark, the city's patron saint. Before 1797 it was the Doge's own chapel. The present building was probably begun in 1063, modelled on a church in Constantinople, and many of its marbles and carvings were brought back from there.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the open paving in the middle of Piazza San Marco, between the Campanile and the basilica. The basilica is about 95 m to the east, so face east and you'll see the whole front.

card.hook: Here's a street where the front doors open straight onto the water, and the traffic is boats. The Grand Canal is Venice showing off, and one bridge gives you the best view of it.
card.stand_here: Stand in the middle of Ponte dell'Accademia and face east, toward the domed church of Santa Maria della Salute. Lean on the side of the bridge to keep your phone steady.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole canal view. Go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to bring the Salute dome closer, or zoom 0.5x if you want the bridge railing and lots of sky.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the dome, then slide the brightness down a little so the sky keeps its colour at sunset.
card.best_time: Go at sunset or blue hour, when the light is lovely. The bridge is very busy in high season, so early or late gives you more room.
card.selfie_here: Try the San Polo side of the canal at Riva del Vin, right by the gondola crossing (the traghetto). Use the front camera, put the gondolas and the Grand Canal behind you, and enjoy a much quieter spot than the Rialto Bridge.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to go down to the eastern bank at the foot of the bridge while you stand on the bridge, so they can shoot low with you, the canal and the dome all in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Ponte dell'Accademia is a public bridge, free to use and open at all hours. If you visit the Rialto Bridge too, it's very slippery, so take care stepping into position.
card.challenge: Keep the dome slightly off-centre and wait for a boat to glide into one third of the frame, then tap the button.
card.good_to_know: The Grand Canal is 3.8 kilometres long and winds through Venice in a big reverse S from the railway station to the basin at San Marco. More than 170 buildings line it, mostly from the 13th to the 18th century, built by noble families who wanted their palazzi to show off their wealth. Ponte dell'Accademia is one of only four bridges over the canal.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the middle of Ponte dell'Accademia and face east, toward the domed church of Santa Maria della Salute. Lean on the side of the bridge to keep your phone steady.

card.hook: La Fenice has burned down twice and each time the city just built it again, which makes the quiet canal behind it feel like a small victory lap.
card.stand_here: Walk around to the back of the theatre on the San Marco side and stand on Rio della Veste, with the theatre to the north-west. Face along the water so the buildings and little bridges frame it on both sides.
card.zoom: Stay at zoom 1x for the canal scene, which keeps the buildings and bridges looking natural. Over on Campo San Fantin, switch to zoom 0.5x if you can't step back far enough to fit the whole front in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the water in the lower third, then tap the water and drag the slider to darker if the sky looks washed out.
card.best_time: Early morning. Photo guides say the canal is nearly empty then, so you get the bridges to yourself.
card.selfie_here: Try the small bridge across the canal from the theatre front. A travel guide says it gives a view of La Fenice reflected in the canal, so use the front camera, switch to zoom 0.5x and keep the theatre over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the bank across the canal near Ponte Maria Callas while you stand on the unnamed bridge two minutes away, next to Ponte dei Callegheri; from the front of the theatre, walk down C. de la Fenice to the right to reach it.
card.rules_and_safety: The canal-side street and the square in front are public, but the theatre interior is only open on tours and for performances, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot of the back canal and one of the front, then spot the Phoenix emblem above the main door and the statues of Dance and Music in their niches.
card.good_to_know: La Fenice means "The Phoenix", named for the company that built it after losing its earlier theatre and wanting to rise again. It opened in May 1792 to a design by Giannantonio Selva, and it burned down in 1836 and again in 1996, each time rebuilt. Many famous operas by Rossini, Bellini, Donizetti and Verdi were first performed here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk around to the back of the theatre on the San Marco side and stand on Rio della Veste, with the theatre to the north-west. Face along the water so the buildings and little bridges frame it on both sides.

The bridge behind La Fenice is unnamed, and the page gives Calle Caotorta as only an approximate address. The Follow Me Away page does not say whether the theatre appears in the photographer's frame, so the ask-someone spot is unconfirmed for showing the whole landmark. The Rio della Veste pages describe it as a photo spot behind the theatre but do not say the theatre is in the frame, so treat it as a second-choice guess. A tour ticket reportedly allows non-commercial photos inside the theatre when no rehearsal is taking place, per TravelPixelz; this is a photography rule, not a selfie-stick rule, so it is not listed under rules.

card.hook: Tucked down a quiet lane near Campo Manin, there's a stone snail climbing up the side of a palace. It's a spiral staircase, and the tight little courtyard it lives in makes it look even taller.
card.stand_here: Stand in Corte Contarina del Bovolo, in the corner of the courtyard furthest from the tower. The tower is to the north-west of you, so face north-west and tilt your phone up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole tower into the tight courtyard. Then try 1x for a closer shot of a few arches, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line one vertical line up with the tower so it stands straight instead of leaning.
card.best_time: Pick a quiet moment in the lane and wait for a gap if people wander into your shot. Aim for a time when some light reaches the upper arches, so they stand out against the shaded walls.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with a view, go up to the small balcony beside the circular belvedere terrace at the top of the staircase. Use the front camera and hold it a little low, so you, the terrace and the view all fit in. St Mark's Campanile stays in sight from the terrace, so try to get it behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the courtyard of Corte del Maltese and frame the staircase head-on, while you pose before you start climbing.
card.rules_and_safety: The single narrow staircase has no separate way down, so don't stop on the steps. Take photos from the openings at each landing, where there's room to stand aside. Be respectful, don't block narrow passages, and follow staff instructions, as rules can change. The top is more than 25 metres up, and looking down isn't recommended if you're afraid of heights.
card.challenge: Get the tower perfectly straight on your gridlines with a sliver of sky above the top arch. Then count how many arches you can fit in one shot.
card.good_to_know: The Scala del Bovolo means 'of the snail'. It was added in 1499 and is believed to be the work of Giorgio Spavento, while the palace itself was designed by Giovanni Candi for the Contarini family. Orson Welles used it as Brabantio's house in his 1952 film of Othello. The staircase has been open to visitors since February 2016, but check the official site before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Corte Contarina del Bovolo, in the corner of the courtyard furthest from the tower. The tower is to the north-west of you, so face north-west and tilt your phone up.

card.hook: Picture a long row of arches with little café tables tucked underneath, and from April to October an orchestra playing on the terrace. Caffè Florian is a postcard before you even lift your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza San Marco, on the open paving in front of the Procuratie Nuove arcade, and face the café's arcaded front. St Mark's Basilica is behind you to the east, so it won't be in this shot.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the café front. If you want more of the arcade in the picture, tap 0.5x.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the arches with the vertical lines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning for a cleaner view before the crowds arrive. Early evening gives you warmer light and a livelier square.
card.selfie_here: Stand by the café's outdoor tables under the striped awnings, with the building's front behind you. Or step under the arches of the arcade, next to the café. Use the front camera and try 0.5x so the arches fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the open square in front of the café's frontage, so the whole building and the square fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open to everyone, but the café is a private business and its interior is for customers. Photography rules can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get every arch in a straight, even row with a table in the foreground and nobody walking through? A short burst of shots gives you a better chance.
card.good_to_know: Caffè Florian opened on 29 December 1720 as "Alla Venezia Trionfante". It soon took the name of its first owner, Floriano Francesconi. It's the oldest coffee house in continuous operation in Italy. Inside there are painted halls, a Hall of Mirrors and an art nouveau room with hand-painted mirrors.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza San Marco, on the open paving in front of the Procuratie Nuove arcade, and face the café's arcaded front. St Mark's Basilica is behind you to the east, so it won't be in this shot.

selfie_spots.detail: On the square, at the café's outdoor tables under the striped awnings, with the building's facade behind you
selfie_spots.why: Guides describe the café's tables spreading into the square, and say the outside of the building photographs well.

card.hook: Everyone on the Ponte dell'Accademia is busy photographing the view, so you get to be the clever one and photograph the bridge itself. It's a big timber arch with a church dome tucked behind it, and hardly anyone shoots it.
card.stand_here: Stand in Campo della Carità, at the Dorsoduro end, then drop down to the bank at the foot of the bridge. Face the bridge and crouch a little so the wooden arch rises above you with the dome of Santa Maria della Salute just behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the bridge with the dome behind it. Go to zoom 0.5x to fit the whole timber structure and some water in one shot, or zoom 2x to 5x to pick out the dome or the wooden detail.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge up with one of the thirds instead of centring it, then tap the sky and slide it a touch darker so it doesn't wash out against the dark wood.
card.best_time: Pick a time when the light is soft rather than harsh, so the timber keeps its detail and the sky stays blue. The bridge can get busy, so give it a few minutes and wait for a gap.
card.selfie_here: Try the bank at the foot of the bridge. Use the front camera, hold it low and crouch so the bridge's wooden structure fills the frame behind you. Nobody has confirmed this as a proper selfie spot, so check your frame on the spot.
card.rules_and_safety: The wooden treads of the bridge can be slippery in winter rain, so wear flat shoes. Walkways beside the water can close during high water in late autumn and winter, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get three layers in one shot: wood in front, water in the middle, dome at the back. Bonus points if a boat drifts through.
card.good_to_know: This is one of only four bridges across the Grand Canal, and it's named after the art academy that once shared the nearby Scuola della Carità with the Gallerie dell'Accademia. The first steel bridge opened in 1854. The wooden one you see now was designed by Eugenio Miozzi and opened in 1933, and plenty of people at the time had hoped for stone.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Campo della Carità, at the Dorsoduro end, then drop down to the bank at the foot of the bridge. Face the bridge and crouch a little so the wooden arch rises above you with the dome of Santa Maria della Salute just behind it.

selfie_spots.detail: on the bank at the bridge's foot, standing low so the bridge structure fills the frame behind you
selfie_spots.why: Localgrapher's photo advice puts the bridge structure with the Salute dome behind the subject, so a visitor standing here would have the landmark behind them, though the page does not describe a selfie.

The 'eastern bank' label comes from one blog and could not be checked against a map. No page names a spot where a passer-by should stand to photograph a visitor with the whole bridge, so I left that null. No page I found mentions selfie-stick rules. card.hook: Picture 98.6 metres of plain brick standing alone in the middle of Venice, and you with a phone that's about 15 centimetres tall. Don't worry, the tower is easy to find and it's very patient.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza San Marco, with the basilica's facade and domes in view. The tower lies to the south-east of you, so face that way and let it rise beside the basilica.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the tower beside the basilica. Tip the phone back to zoom 0.5x if you want the whole height in one go, or try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the belfry and the golden weather vane.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the tower up with a vertical line and keep the phone level so the sides don't lean in. Then tap the brick and drag the slider to make it a little darker, so the sky stays blue and the gold on top keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning is calmest. The light is softer and fewer people wander through your frame.
card.selfie_here: Try the Piazzetta San Marco, the arm of the square next to Piazza San Marco, where the tower fills the view behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, and keep the Campanile over your shoulder. The open square also works if you face the basilica end so the tower stays in the scene.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand under the arcade of the Procuratie Nuove colonnade on the south side of the square and shoot diagonally across it, while you stand out in the square so you and the whole tower fit in one frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The square is open public space, but climbing the tower is a paid, ticketed visit. It can close in high winds or cold weather, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Fit the whole tower in the frame with the sky filling the top, then zoom in and catch the golden archangel Gabriel on the weather vane.
card.good_to_know: The Campanile is the bell tower of St Mark's Basilica and the tallest structure in Venice. It began in the early tenth century as a watchtower and a landmark for ships coming into the harbour. The tower you see today is a reconstruction finished in 1912, after the earlier one collapsed in 1902.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza San Marco, with the basilica's facade and domes in view. The tower lies to the south-east of you, so face that way and let it rise beside the basilica.

card.hook: Picture a big white dome sitting all by itself at the end of the Grand Canal, as if the whole canal was built to show it off. That's the Salute, and it really does look this good from the bridge.
card.stand_here: Go to the top of Ponte dell'Accademia and stand at the western railing. Look down the Grand Canal: the church is about 450 m to the east of the bridge in a straight line, with the dome framed at the far end of the water.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get the canal, the palaces and the dome together. Then try zoom 2x for a tighter shot of the domes. Skip zoom 0.5x here, because it makes the church look small and far away.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky near the dome, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky keeps its colour and the white stone doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Sunset and blue hour are the favourites, but the bridge gets very busy and you may have to jostle for railing space. For fewer people, one local photographer's guide suggests about 6:45 to 7:30 AM in December and January. Check sunrise and sunset times for your actual date.
card.selfie_here: Walk the stone promenade at Punta della Dogana round to the east side. Turn your back to the Salute, face the open lagoon and San Marco, and use the front camera so the church sits over your shoulder. Evening golden hour is the best light there. The church's own steps are another option, with the façade behind you for a close-up selfie.
card.ask_someone: Near the Gondola Dogana Vallaresso station on the pier across the Grand Canal, sit on the pier edge in the corner facing the church, and ask a passer-by to stand behind you so the church shows beyond.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge and canal-side views are open public space, but the Salute is a working church. Check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and dress.
card.challenge: Be patient and spot your gap at the railing, then grab one shot with the dome sitting near an upper gridline corner and the canal running in from the lower corner.
card.good_to_know: Venice vowed to build the Salute after the plague of 1630, which killed nearly a third of the city's people. Baldassare Longhena designed it, work began in 1631 and it was finished in 1681. It stands on a platform of about a million wooden piles. Every 21 November a temporary pontoon bridge crosses the Grand Canal to the church for the Festa della Madonna della Salute.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the top of Ponte dell'Accademia and stand at the western railing. Look down the Grand Canal: the church is about 450 m to the east of the bridge in a straight line, with the dome framed at the far end of the water.

selfie_spots.why: Standing with your back to the basilica puts it directly behind you, and the guide's best light window is the evening golden hour.

card.hook: Look up and count the colours: blue and gold clock face, a starry blue sky behind a winged lion, and two bronze Moors on the roof waiting to strike the hour. This tower packs a lot into one frame.
card.stand_here: Stand in Piazza San Marco at the far end of the square, near the Basilica, and face northeast toward the tower. The open space lets you fit the whole thing in with the clock and the Moors above the archway.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole tower with some square in front. If scaffolding or crowds get in the way, drop to 0.5x. Then zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the clock face, the Lion and the Moors.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so it stands straight, then tap the clock face and drag the brightness down a touch to keep the blue and gold rich.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the evening for softer light and fewer people. If the evening light gets dim, try night mode and hold the phone very still.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the square in front of the gold, zodiac-decorated clock face with the tower behind you. Or stand on the square side of the archway where the Merceria comes out, so the tower rises behind you. Use the front camera, switch to the wider option (0.5x) if your phone has one, and keep the tower over your shoulder. Check both spots on the day, since crowds and scaffolding can change the view.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the far end of the square near St Mark's Basilica and shoot back toward the tower while you stand in front of it, so the whole tower fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: There may be scaffolding in the square, so check how it looks on the day. Going inside or up to the terrace is only possible on advance-booked guided tours, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the tower dead straight on a grid line, then zoom in and catch the two Moors on the roof like you've spotted them sneaking about.
card.good_to_know: The tower and clock date from the 1490s, and the clock opened on 1 February 1499. The two bronze Moors strike the hours on a bell cast in 1497. The clock face shows a marble ring of the 24 hours, the zodiac, a sun pointer and a little earth and moon at the centre.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Piazza San Marco at the far end of the square, near the Basilica, and face northeast toward the tower. The open space lets you fit the whole thing in with the clock and the Moors above the archway.

selfie_spots.why: One guide calls the tower's façade a must-photo, and standing in front of it puts the tower behind you in the frame.

card.hook: Ca' d'Oro means "House of Gold", and the whole front is one big lacy pattern, with boats drifting past like they were hired for the shot. You'll want to see it straight on.
card.stand_here: Go to the far end of Riva de l'Ogio, near Calle del Campaniel, and step onto the wooden pontoon that reaches out onto the Grand Canal. Face across the water and the whole palace sits right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole palace from across the water. Go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the loggia arches and the roofline pinnacles. Use 0.5x only if you want more water and sky, because it makes the palace look smaller and bends the edges.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line up the roofline with a horizontal line so the facade doesn't lean, and leave a strip of water at the bottom for boat reflections.
card.best_time: Guides suggest late afternoon light for the facade, but that isn't tied to this exact spot. Check the light on the day, and if the front is in deep shade, move.
card.selfie_here: Try the quay at the Ca' d'Oro vaporetto stop, where the palace facade is in view. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the palace over your shoulder. No guide calls it a selfie spot, so treat it as a good one to test.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the land end of the wooden pontoon near Calle del Campaniel while you stand out on the pontoon with the palace across the water behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules inside the gallery are conflicting (one blog says photos were banned indoors, but it may be out of date), so check the signs when you arrive. The loggia is part of the ticketed museum.
card.challenge: Wait for a boat to glide into that strip of water at the bottom of your frame, then snap it. Bonus points if it lines up with the middle of the palace.
card.good_to_know: Ca' d'Oro was built between 1421 and 1437 for Marino Contarini. It takes its name from the gilding and colour that once decorated its walls. Today it's a museum, the Galleria Giorgio Franchetti alla Ca' d'Oro, open since 1927.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Go to the far end of Riva de l'Ogio, near Calle del Campaniel, and step onto the wooden pontoon that reaches out onto the Grand Canal. Face across the water and the whole palace sits right in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a shop where you look up and see four floors of arches stacked around you, like a very fancy stadium for merchants. That's the Fondaco dei Tedeschi, right beside the Rialto Bridge.
card.stand_here: The phone icon on the map puts you at the heart of the Fondaco dei Tedeschi, around its big central courtyard. Stand there and look up and around at the floors, rather than at one flat wall.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the courtyard and its layers of arches in one shot. Switch to 1x for a more natural view, then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for details high up, like the clock and the roofline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line them up with the arches and the building's vertical edges so everything stays nice and straight.
card.best_time: Soft, even daylight works best, like a bright overcast day or any time outside the middle of the day. Going early may mean a quieter courtyard, but check the official site for opening times first.
card.selfie_here: Try Calle del Fontego dei Tedeschi, on the calle beside the Fondaco near the Rialto Bridge end, just outside Ristorante Al Buso. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the street behind your shoulder, and check your screen to see how much of the building sneaks in, because we can't promise the Fondaco will be in the frame.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the Rialto Bridge and ask a passer-by for a wide shot, so the canal façade of the Fondaco shows across the water with you in front.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a department store now, so some areas may have access limits. Check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you catch three levels of arches in one straight-lined shot, then find a sphere-topped roofline merlon to zoom in on?
card.good_to_know: The first building here dates from 1228 and was the hostel and warehouse of Venice's German merchants. After a fire in 1505 it was rebuilt in Renaissance style between 1505 and 1508. The façades were once frescoed, but only faint fragments survive, so don't expect colour on the walls.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: The phone icon on the map puts you at the heart of the Fondaco dei Tedeschi, around its big central courtyard. Stand there and look up and around at the floors, rather than at one flat wall.

selfie_research.notes: Rooftop terrace status conflicts: rialto-bridge.com (2026 status page) and cityscrolls say the store and terrace have been closed since spring 2025, and europeforvisitors calls the closure permanent. Other pages (localgrapher, a webcam page, airial) still describe it as open with free online booking. Treat the terrace as closed unless confirmed on site, so I did not list it as a selfie spot. No page places a visitor with the Fondaco directly behind them, so the Calle del Fontego spot is a weak match. The ask-someone spot is the Rialto Bridge, but no source says how much of the whole building fits in that frame. Sources give no selfie stick or tripod rules.

card.hook: Everyone queues up for Ca' Pesaro from the Grand Canal. Here's a quieter trick: slip down a narrow side canal and watch the big Baroque palace fill the far end of the water like a surprise at the end of a corridor.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ponte del Forner, the bridge over Rio de la Pergola. From the Grand Canal frontage of Ca' Pesaro, walk south-west along the side canal, about 250 m on foot. Turn around and face north-east, and the palace is right there with the Grand Canal just beyond.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the canal, the water and the palace at the far end. Try 0.5x if you want the bridge edge and canal walls as a frame, or 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pull the palace closer.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the palace, then slide the brightness down a little so the pale marble keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, when the soft light flatters pale stone. If people are crossing the bridge, wait for a gap and take your time.
card.selfie_here: Turn on the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone slightly higher than your face. Turn so the palace sits over your shoulder and the canal runs behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The view from the bridge is public. Inside the gallery, selfie sticks, flash and video aren't allowed, though photographing the artworks is fine. Entry may be ticketed and photo rules can change by room, so check the signs.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, put the canal dead centre and the palace on a vertical line, then see if you can get the water to lead the eye straight to it with no wobbly horizon.
card.good_to_know: Baldassarre Longhena began the palace in 1659. He also designed the church of the Salute and Ca' Rezzonico, but died before Ca' Pesaro was finished. Gian Antonio Gaspari completed it in 1710. In 1898 Duchess Felicita Bevilacqua La Masa left it to the city, and today it's Venice's modern art museum, home to Klimt's Judith II.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ponte del Forner, the bridge over Rio de la Pergola. From the Grand Canal frontage of Ca' Pesaro, walk south-west along the side canal, about 250 m on foot. Turn around and face north-east, and the palace is right there with the Grand Canal just beyond.

ask_someone_spot.detail: Stand on the bridge and frame the canal running toward the Grand Canal, where Ca' Pesaro is visible at the far end. The source describes a photo of the canal and Ca' Pesaro taken from this bridge, not a shot of a visitor posing in front of the palace.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot where visitors pose with Ca' Pesaro behind them, so selfie_spots is empty rather than guessed. The Rio di Noale is named by several pages as a good view of the palace (for example, the canal's view south to Ca' Pesaro, best at dusk), but those pages describe photographing the building, not a visitor's selfie, so I did not list it. The Ponte del Forner entry is the only named spot for a passer-by shot, and the source confirms the view of the canal and palace, not a framed photo of a visitor with the whole palace. The rule about selfie poles and tripods applies to the gallery interior per the visit-venice-italy page, and I found no outdoor rule. Source coordinates for the Ponte del Forner photo point are about 45.44065, 12.33089, which is close to the given landmark position but I did not verify the bridge's exact location on a map.

card.hook: Imagine a jewellery box that someone set down beside a canal and forgot to pick up. That's Santa Maria dei Miracoli, the "marble church" of Cannaregio, with walls in pale and coloured marble.
card.stand_here: Stand on Ponte dei Miracoli, the small bridge directly across the rio from the church. Face the marble facade so the canal fills the bottom of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole front with water in front of it. If you're squeezed for space, try 0.5x, but it can make the building lean. Then go to 2x for the round windows, the curved top and the marble patterns.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line them up with the church's straight vertical edges, and keep your phone level so the walls don't tilt.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning if you can, when the bridge is usually quieter. Soft, even daylight shows off the marble colours best.
card.selfie_here: Try the small canal bridge facing the marble facade, near the church's square. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and see if you can fit the church behind your shoulder. Check the framing on the spot, as it can be tricky.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you with the church, ask someone in Campo Santa Maria Nova (over the bridge) to shoot back across the Rio dei Miracoli, though from there they may catch the back of the church (the apse) rather than the full front.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside from the public bridges and lanes. Inside, it's a place of worship, and what's allowed isn't clear, so check the signs and the official site before you take your phone out.
card.challenge: Hunt for the inlaid shapes in the facade: a square, a cross, a star and a wheel. Can you get all four in one shot?
card.good_to_know: Pietro Lombardo designed the church in 1481 with his sons Tullio and Antonio, and it was finished in 1489. It was built to house a painting of the Madonna that local people thought was miraculous. It was restored between 1990 and 1997, which is why the marble looks so clean and bright.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Ponte dei Miracoli, the small bridge directly across the rio from the church. Face the marble facade so the canal fills the bottom of your frame.

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot was supported by a page. The bridge source says it gives a good view of the facade but does not say where to stand so the church is behind the visitor, so check that framing on site. The ask-someone spot is a campo view of the apse across the canal, not clearly the full facade, so it may not show the whole church. The inside-photography rules conflict, so check on arrival. No page mentioned selfie sticks or tripods, and no page gave a safety point.
